titre: Ludwik Fleck: A Scientific Fact Has a History
accroche: Twenty-seven years before Kuhn, a microbiologist from Lwów argued that a scientific fact is built by many people, without anyone having intended it to be so.
contenu_vulgarise:
Bring a layperson into a laboratory and ask them to describe the experiment under way. They will produce a long description, full of incidental details, and retain nothing of what the researcher considers essential. To them, there is only chaos. The specialist, by contrast, sees a form at once.

This scene comes from Ludwik Fleck (1896-1961), a Polish-Jewish microbiologist from Lwów, who published in Basel in 1935 *Entstehung und Entwicklung einer wissenschaftlichen Tatsache*, “genesis and development of a scientific fact.” His central idea comes down to an inversion. Empiricists said that nothing is in the mind that was not first in the senses. Fleck answers that nothing is in the senses that was not first in the mind: to see, one must have learned to see, in contact with those who already see. A group that shares this way of seeing forms a “thought collective,” and the way of seeing it has given itself is a “thought style.”

## A syphilis test as evidence

Fleck studies a specific case, the Wassermann reaction, the blood test for syphilis. He shows that no one ever decided to invent it as it is. Syphilis was then a shameful disease, social pressure was strong, and the German government organized research teams. The researchers started from an old, vague idea, that of a “syphilitic blood,” of which nothing would remain in the final test. They read one another, answer one another, misunderstand one another, and words change meaning as they pass from one person to the next. Fifteen years later, Wassermann himself no longer remembers a winding path, but a straight road, stretched toward a goal. The result is a body of knowledge that no one had foreseen or intended.

## What this shifts

Popularizations and textbooks state facts without caution. Fleck observes that this tone passes off as a discovery what was constructed: as the social distance grows between the author and the readers, the creator becomes a mere discoverer, and knowledge seems to exist with no one having made it.

The book went almost unnoticed. In 1962, in the preface to *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions*, Thomas Kuhn describes it as an almost unknown monograph that anticipates many of his own ideas, and says he is indebted to this work and to conversations in more ways than he can account for. The two authors do not say the same thing: Fleck focuses on how a fact is made, Kuhn on how a paradigm collapses.

Fleck's thesis is radical. According to the entry of the *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* that summarizes it, what we call facts are social constructions: only what is true for a culture is true for nature. We look with our own eyes, he writes, but we see with those of the collective to which we belong.

repere.texte: In 1962, in the preface to The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, Thomas Kuhn cites Ludwik Fleck's monograph, Entstehung und Entwicklung einer wissenschaftlichen Tatsache (Basel, 1935), as an essay that anticipates many of his own ideas, and which he says he came across thanks to Harvard's Society of Fellows.
repere.source: Thomas S. Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, preface, 2nd ed., University of Chicago Press, 1970

carte.punch: No one decided what the Wassermann test is: it arises in part from misunderstandings.
carte.idee: In 1935, the microbiologist Ludwik Fleck reconstructs the genesis of the syphilis test: social pressure, a vague idea that did not survive, misunderstandings among researchers. A scientific fact, he says, arises from a collective, and its outcome was foreseen by no one.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biography, including his deportation to Auschwitz and then Buchenwald, and the first English translation of his book in 1979 from University of Chicago Press, with a preface by Kuhn.

quiz.question: According to Fleck, why does a layperson placed in a laboratory fail to retain the essence of the experiment?
choix: Because the instruments are too complex for them to understand how they work without theoretical training
Because the researchers deliberately omit the steps that might give away their methods
Because seeing means recognizing forms learned from a collective, and they have not learned them
Because their perception, less trained for precision, records fewer details than the researcher's
quiz.explication: For Fleck, one sees only what one has learned to see in contact with a thought collective. The layperson, on the contrary, describes many details, but with no hierarchy: what is missing is the learning that makes a form emerge from chaos, and neither the instruments, nor secrecy, nor the precision of perception changes that.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which medical test does Fleck take as a case study to show how a scientific fact arises?
choix: The Wassermann reaction test, for diagnosing syphilis
The tuberculin test, for diagnosing tuberculosis
The ABO test, for determining blood groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fleck studies the genesis of the Wassermann reaction, the blood test for syphilis, to show that no researcher alone decided its final form.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Fleck call a group of researchers that shares the same way of seeing an experiment?
choix: A scientific paradigm, a concept Kuhn would develop decades later
A thought collective, endowed with a thought style
A doctrinal school, organized around a single master
A community of proof, gathered around the same experimental protocol
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fleck calls the group that shares a way of seeing a “thought collective,” and that way of seeing itself a “thought style”; “paradigm” is the word Kuhn would coin later, for a different idea.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Thomas Kuhn say, in the 1962 preface to his own book, about Fleck's monograph?
choix: That he discovered it after publishing his own thesis, without having read it beforehand
That it defends a thesis he himself considers to have since been refuted
That it is an almost unknown monograph that anticipates many of his own ideas
That it deals with a subject too remote from his own to be compared
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kuhn writes that Fleck's monograph, almost unknown, anticipates many of his own ideas, and says he is indebted to these readings in more ways than he can account for.
